investigations.name: distance-immigration
investigations.description:
Faithful port of IslandManager.simulate's migration loop: for each ordered
island pair (i, j), with probability migration_rate(d_ij) a random present
species moves one individual i -> j. This study isolates the MigrationProcess
coupler: it validates the distance kernel (the colonization/immigration side of
island biogeography) and the conservation law that makes migration a genuine
exchange rather than a source/sink. Islands are held at full occupancy so the
measured immigration reflects the geometry, not transient population collapse.
investigations.title: Isolation reduces colonization; migration conserves individuals
investigations.objective:
Does the distance-decaying migration kernel (migration_rate = 1/(1+distance))
reproduce the immigration side of MacArthur-Wilson theory — more isolated
islands receive fewer colonists — and does inter-island migration conserve
individuals exactly?

investigations.name: general-dynamic-model
investigations.description:
This study extends the static MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium
(mw-equilibrium-reproduction) with the single ingredient Whittaker, Triantis
& Ladle (2008, citekey whittaker2008general) argue is decisive for oceanic
(volcanic) islands: island ontogeny. The GeneralDynamicModelProcess is
deliberately identical to MacArthurWilsonEquilibriumProcess except that the
island's area traces a humped life-cycle A(t), so the per-species extinction
probability e(t) = extinction_base*(ref_area/A(t))^area_exponent is lowest at
the island's prime and rises again as it erodes. Three islands are staggered
along a t_peak age gradient (120/150/180) so a single run shows young, mid-life
and old islands peaking at different times — the GDM's space-for-time logic.
The headline result is the emergent humped richness trajectory, the GDM's
central qualitative departure from the 1967 equilibrium theory.
investigations.title: General Dynamic Model: does island ontogeny make richness hump then decline?
investigations.objective:
Under the General Dynamic Model of oceanic island biogeography (Whittaker,
Triantis & Ladle 2008), an island's area is not static: it is born, grows as
it is built up, then subsides and erodes over geological time. When area rises
then erodes (island ontogeny), does species richness OVERSHOOT and then
DECLINE — a humped trajectory — unlike the flat static-area MacArthur-Wilson
equilibrium?

investigations.name: island-archipelago
investigations.description:
Faithful port of experiments/island_lotka_volterra.py. Area appears only as
the per-island carrying capacity in the discrete LV update's rescale step.
The study separates the two things "area effect" could mean and shows the
model couples area to abundance (exactly) but not to richness (random
competition collapses each island to a couple of dominant species). Study 3
(island-food-web) shows that trophic interaction structure is what restores
the area-richness relationship.
investigations.title: Carrying capacity sets abundance, not richness
investigations.objective:
In the Lotka-Volterra island model, does island area control the equilibrium
state — and if so, which quantity: total abundance, species richness, or both?

investigations.name: island-food-web
investigations.description:
Faithful port of experiments/island_food_web.py (generate_food_web +
generate_interaction_matrix_from_food_web). The ONLY change from Study 1 is
the interaction matrix; the islands, migration coupler, and dynamics are
identical. The contrast isolates interaction STRUCTURE as the cause of the
species-area law: random competition (Study 1) destroys it, trophic structure
(this study) restores it.
investigations.title: Trophic structure restores the species-area law
investigations.objective:
Does replacing the random interaction matrix with a trophic food web
(producers -> primary -> secondary consumers, antisymmetric predator-prey
couplings) change whether the model reproduces the classic species-area
relationship of island biogeography?

investigations.name: microbial-island-biogeography
investigations.description:
Microbial island biogeography (martiny2006microbial; hanson2012beyond) revived
the MacArthur-Wilson framework for microbes and found that the classic laws
hold in sign but differ sharply in degree. Horner-Devine et al. (2004,
hornerdevine2004taxa) measured a shallow taxa-area slope z ~ 0.02-0.1 for salt-
marsh sediment bacteria; Bell et al. (2005, bell2005islands) found a positive
but low z for bacteria in water-filled tree holes. The flatness is attributed
to a vast species pool (islands never saturate it), high passive dispersal
(little colonization limitation), and rapid local turnover.
This study does not build a new model: it reuses the already-validated
mw_equilibrium process in a microbial parameter regime (the microbial_island
composite) and compares it, on the same area gradient, to the macro regime the
species-area-and-isolation study calibrated. The microbial regime's shallow
area-extinction exponent reproduces the observed flat taxa-area slope while the
high per-taxon rates reproduce the fast turnover. The Earth Microbiome Project
(global 16S taxa-area surveys) and the tree-hole bacterial datasets
(bell2005islands) are the natural empirical validation targets for the measured
z and turnover. Builds on species-area-and-isolation, which established that the
process sits on the equilibrium rate curves and gives z ~ 0.12 in the macro
regime.
investigations.title: Does the taxa-area relationship hold for microbes — and flatten?
investigations.objective:
Does the taxa-area relationship — the microbial analogue of the species-area
law — hold under the MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium model when it is run in a
microbial regime, and is its slope z flatter than for macro-organisms?

investigations.name: mw-equilibrium-reproduction
investigations.description:
This study reproduces the ORIGINAL theory directly, as a counterpart to the
mechanistic Lotka-Volterra port used elsewhere in this investigation. The
MacArthurWilsonEquilibriumProcess treats each species as present/absent and
draws colonization/extinction from the isolation- and area-dependent rates of
The Theory of Island Biogeography. A single run over an area gradient yields
the rate-crossing equilibrium, the approach to S*, and turnover at constant
richness — the three signatures of the 1967 monograph.
investigations.title: Reproducing the MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium: rate crossing + turnover
investigations.objective:
Does a direct, phenomenological implementation of the original theory of
island biogeography (MacArthur & Wilson 1963, 1967) reproduce its three core
claims — (1) species richness relaxes to the equilibrium S* where the
immigration and extinction rate curves cross, (2) richness tracks the analytic
S* = P*c/(c+e) across islands, and (3) species identity turns over while
richness stays constant?

investigations.name: neutral-vs-equilibrium
investigations.description:
This study adds Hubbell's (2001) *Unified Neutral Theory of Biodiversity and
Biogeography* (citekey hubbell2001unified) as a mechanistic counterpoint to the
already-reproduced MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium model. The
NeutralMetacommunityProcess assumes strict ecological equivalence: every
individual has identical birth/death/dispersal rates, and local diversity is a
dynamic balance between demographic drift in a finite zero-sum community and
immigration from the metacommunity. The metacommunity is treated as a uniform
pool, so the skewed local species-abundance distribution that appears is a pure
dispersal-drift result. By driving both the neutral and the equilibrium
composites over an identical area gradient we test whether two unrelated
mechanisms converge on the same macroecological law (a positive SAR) — a classic
question in community ecology (neutral theory as a null model for niche-based
equilibrium theory).
investigations.title: Neutral vs equilibrium: do dispersal-drift and colonization-extinction predict the same macroecology?
investigations.objective:
Hubbell's (2001) neutral theory and MacArthur & Wilson's (1967) equilibrium
theory derive island diversity from completely different mechanisms — neutral
dispersal-drift among ecologically equivalent individuals in a fixed-size local
community, versus per-species colonization/extinction rates set by area and
isolation. Do these two mechanisms nonetheless predict the SAME emergent
macroecology — specifically, do both produce a positive species-area
relationship S ∝ A^z, and what does the neutral local species-abundance
distribution look like?

investigations.name: rescue-effect
investigations.description:
This study extends the independent-curves MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium
(mw-equilibrium-reproduction) with the rescue effect of Brown & Kodric-Brown
(1977), who found that immigration to boulder-field "islands" propped up
resident populations and flattened the expected species-area/isolation
relationships. The RescueEffectProcess keeps every rule of
MacArthurWilsonEquilibriumProcess but lets the incoming colonization pressure
also rescue present species from extinction, coupling the two rate curves. A
single run sweeps rescue strength at fixed area and isolation, isolating the
coupling as the only varying quantity.
investigations.title: The rescue effect: immigration lowers extinction (Brown & Kodric-Brown 1977)
investigations.objective:
In the canonical MacArthur-Wilson model the immigration curve I(S)=(P-S)c and
the extinction curve E(S)=S*e are independent. Brown & Kodric-Brown (1977;
citekey brown1977turnover) argued they are not: a population fed by immigrant
propagules is less likely to blink out, so immigration also *lowers*
extinction — the rescue effect. How does coupling the two curves this way
raise equilibrium richness and reduce turnover compared to the
independent-curves baseline?

investigations.name: species-area-and-isolation
investigations.description:
This study turns the two qualitative predictions of island biogeography into
measured laws using the mw_equilibrium composite. The area gradient isolates
the extinction side (larger islands lose species less often -> more species);
the distance gradient isolates the colonization side (farther islands receive
fewer colonists -> fewer species). It builds on mw-equilibrium-reproduction,
which established that the process sits on the equilibrium rate curves.
investigations.title: The species-area law and the isolation gradient
investigations.objective:
Under the canonical MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium model, do the two central
predictions emerge as quantitative laws — (1) equilibrium richness grows with
island area as a power law S ~ A^z (Arrhenius 1921; Preston 1962), and (2)
equilibrium richness declines monotonically with isolation distance?
